A theme that will later unfold concerns the use of coordinate systems. We can identify the point $(x,y)$ with the tip of the vector $\left[\begin{array}{r}x\\y\end{array}\right]$, drawn emanating from the origin. We can then think of the usual Cartesian coordinate system in terms of linear combinations of the vectors $$ \evec_1 = \left[\begin{array}{r} 1 \\ 0 \end{array}\right], \evec_2 = \left[\begin{array}{r} 0 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]. $$ For instance, the point $(2,-3)$ is identified with the vector $$\left[\begin{array}{r} 2 \\ -3 \end{array}\right] = 2\evec_1 - 3\evec_2, $$ as shown on the left in [fig-ex-coords-1].

The usual Cartesian coordinate system, defined by the vectors $\evec_1$ and $\evec_2$, is shown on the left along with the representation of the point $(2,-3)$. The right shows a nonstandard coordinate system defined by vectors $\vvec_1$ and $\vvec_2$.

If instead we have vectors $$ \vvec_1 = \left[\begin{array}{r} 2 \\ 1 \end{array}\right], \vvec_2 = \left[\begin{array}{r} 1 \\ 2 \end{array}\right] $$ , we may define a new coordinate system in which a point $\{c,d\}$ will correspond to the vector $$ c\vvec_1 + d\vvec_2 $$ . For instance, the point $\{2,-3\}$ is shown on the right side of [fig-ex-coords-1].

Write the point $\{2,-3\}$ in standard coordinates; that is, find $x$ and $y$ such that $$ (x,y) = \{2,-3\} $$ .

Write the point $(2,-3)$ in the new coordinate system; that is, find $c$ and $d$ such that $$ \{c,d\} = (2,-3) $$ .

Convert a general point $\{c,d\}$, expressed in the new coordinate system, into standard Cartesian coordinates $(x,y)$.

What is the general strategy for converting a point from standard Cartesian coordinates $(x,y)$ to the new coordinates $\{c,d\}$? Actually implementing this strategy in general may take a bit of work so just describe the strategy. We will study this in more detail later.

In this activity, we will find the determinant of some simple $2\times2$ matrices and discover some important properties of determinants.

The geometric meaning of the determinant of a matrix.

Use the diagram to find the determinant of the matrix $\left[\begin{array}{rr} -\frac12 \amp 0 \\ 0 \amp 2 \end{array}\right]$. Along with [example-det-identity], what does this lead you to believe is generally true about the determinant of a diagonal matrix?

Use the diagram to find the determinant of the matrix $\left[\begin{array}{rr} 0 \amp 1 \\ 1 \amp 0 \\ \end{array}\right]$. What is the geometric effect of the matrix transformation defined by this matrix?

Use the diagram to find the determinant of the matrix $\left[\begin{array}{rr} 2 \amp 1 \\ 0 \amp 1 \\ \end{array}\right]$. More generally, what do you notice about the determinant of any matrix of the form $\left[\begin{array}{rr} 2 \amp k \\ 0 \amp 1 \\ \end{array}\right]$? What does this say about the determinant of an upper triangular matrix?

Use the diagram to find the determinant of any matrix of the form $\left[\begin{array}{rr} 2 \amp 0 \\ k \amp 1 \\ \end{array}\right]$. What does this say about the determinant of a lower triangular matrix?

Use the diagram to find the determinant of the matrix $\left[\begin{array}{rr} 1 \amp -1 \\ -2 \amp 2 \\ \end{array}\right]$. In general, what is the determinant of a matrix whose columns are linearly dependent?

Consider the matrices $$ A = \left[\begin{array}{rr} 2 \amp 1 \\ 2 \amp -1 \\ \end{array}\right],~~~ B = \left[\begin{array}{rr} 1 \amp 0 \\ 0 \amp 2 \\ \end{array}\right] $$ . Use the diagram to find the determinants of $A$, $B$, and $AB$. What does this suggest is generally true about the relationship of $\det(AB)$ to $\det(A)$ and $\det(B)$?
